items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then you worked with Charlie Barnet. You recorded with him a year later and sat in with his band, playing trumpet.

ctx.x: . . . and talk about . . . oh, before we do that, we’re still working with 1933 and your recordings, and it struck me, we mentioned there was one integrated session of the Chocolate Dandies with that title—anachronistic title, oddly enough; it was an integrated band—and later that year you also recorded with Mez Mezro and his orchestra. I believe that was an offshoot of some grandiose idea he had to tour with an interracial group, which never came to fruition, but this was sort of a spin-off from that. Then you…
[unclear], was that one of the songs?

items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: Benny Carter contributed a couple of things [arrangements]... I had Billy in New York... Benny Carter contributed a couple of things.

ctx.x: Gee, that's great. Who were playing at the other hotels in New York around that time?

Well, let's see, Benny Goodman was trying to have a band at Billy Rose's joint on 53rd Street there, which is now the Hammerstein Theater, and he was having a rough time. I remember I even gave him a couple of arrangements. And he and Benny Carter -- and I remember this as clearly as though it was right now. Were rather disgusted with the reception of jazz, you know, or of big band jazz particularly, and jazz in general, and we sat one time at a table there at the Park Central, plotting a European -- we were all…

But nothing ever came of it because Benny you know, managed to get going and he -- well, you know, a lot of things are talked of that never happen. But I remember talking about it. Of course every band in New York that was any kind of a band at all had a Benny Carter arrangement in the book. He wrote more arrangements that he was not paid for, because he had a copyist by the name of Jack Mazel, or Meizel, and every time Benny would make an arrangement Jack would make an extra copy for himself. Jack's room was…
